Q134290371.summary: Christ sits enthroned within a pointed mandorla, blessing with his right hand and holding a book, at the centre of a tall ivory panel. Around him the four evangelists sit at their desks writing, each accompanied by his winged symbol in a roundel, while the vertical and horizontal bands are inscribed LUX, LEX, REX and PAX: light, law, king and peace. The plaque, probably made for a Gospel book cover, presents Christ as the source of the four Gospels.
facts: The museum label (as recorded in the photograph's title) attributes the plaque to Cologne, 960–980.
The four words on the cross-shaped bands, LUX, LEX, REX and PAX, are carved directly on the plaque and frame the mandorla on all four sides.
Q134290371.notes: Inv. Kg 54:209. Title was only an inventory label. Details rest on the museum label as transcribed in the Commons filename; no online museum record was found.

cur:catacombs2-ravenna-constantius-iii-l.summary: In a shallow, worn relief on the front, the Lamb of God, its head encircled by a nimbus, stands on a small mound between other lambs, with palm trees at each end. The image of Christ as the sacrificed and victorious Lamb, surrounded by his flock, sums up the hope of the dead in a few quiet forms. Chi-Rho monograms mark the acroteria of the lid.
facts: Tradition associates the sarcophagi in the mausoleum with Galla Placidia, her husband Constantius III and her brother Honorius, but Italian Wikipedia notes that this rests on oral tradition recorded by Agnellus, and Galla Placidia probably died and was buried in Rome in 450.
The mausoleum's three marble sarcophagi stand at the ends of its arms; Commons dates this one to the late 5th or early 6th century.
cur:catacombs2-ravenna-constantius-iii-l.notes: Christ is represented symbolically, as the nimbed Lamb.

cur:manuscripts-st-gall-gospels-last-jud.summary: In the upper register Christ appears in half-length, haloed and frontal, holding a tall cross-staff and an open book, between two angels blowing long trumpets. Below, twelve apostles in two rows look up toward him, each holding a book. It is a concise Insular image of the Second Coming, facing the Crucifixion on the opposite page.
facts: The manuscript's twelve decorated pages include evangelist portraits, a carpet page and this closing pair of Crucifixion and Last Judgement.
Images are provided by e-codices, the Virtual Manuscript Library of Switzerland, under a CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.
cur:manuscripts-st-gall-gospels-last-jud.notes: Image from e-codices (not Commons); licence CC BY-NC 4.0 per the e-codices IIIF manifest.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-104-chris.summary: The psalmist stands among 'the seed of Abraham' and raises his hands to the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who sits in a globe-mandorla with two angels and holds out a scroll, his covenant, toward three figures probably meant as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Around them the drawing recalls the history of Israel told in the psalm. The scene places the covenant in the hands of Christ.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-104-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-126-chris.summary: Inside a long wall the bearded psalmist, followed by armed men and the faithful, points to the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who stands with three angels beyond a hill holding shield and spear in one hand and a trowel and plumb line in the other: 'except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it'. Watchmen along the wall watch in vain, and the moon and stars mark the hours before dawn. It is the upper drawing of folio 73v.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-126-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-adoration-magi.summary: Under an arcade the Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ child on her lap, and the Magi approach from the left with their gifts, a star shining above. The architecture frames the scene like a palace hall, so that the homage of the kings becomes a court ceremony — fitting in a book made for an emperor.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
The Bayerische Staatsbibliothek has published the whole manuscript online with a Public Domain Mark, so every page can be studied in detail.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-adoration-magi.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 61); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-zeno-anast.summary: The risen Christ, haloed and surrounded by streaming rays, strides into the underworld to rescue the righteous; the heads of Adam, Eve and other figures turn towards him. The Anastasis, the Byzantine image of the Resurrection, was still new in Western art in the 9th century, and this panel is one of its earliest appearances in Rome.
facts: The Chapel of Saint Zeno was built by Pope Paschal I (817–824) as a funerary chapel for his mother, Theodora; its walls and vault are almost entirely clad in gold-ground mosaic.
In Byzantine tradition the Anastasis, Christ's descent to free Adam and Eve, became the standard image of the Resurrection.

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Basilica of Saint Praxedes (Rome) - Chapel of Saint Zeno

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-zeno-anast.notes: The image shows only part of the panel. The date of this panel within the chapel's decoration is not certain; it is usually assigned to Paschal I's campaign.

Q116245184.summary: This slender ivory leaf, once the wing of a small Byzantine triptych, carries three scenes stacked one above another. At the top the Virgin of the Annunciation stands before an architectural backdrop; in the centre Christ hangs on the cross with a mourner beside him; and at the bottom the angel sits upon the empty tomb, announcing the Resurrection. Read from top to bottom, the little panel traces the whole arc of salvation, from the Incarnation to Easter morning.
facts: The Met describes the panel as a fragmentary door whose interior shows the Virgin of the Annunciation, the Crucifixion and the angel seated on Christ's tomb.
It is a small object, only about 19.3 cm high and 4.6 cm wide, and is dated 970–1030; it was probably carved in Constantinople.
